cultivar: Song Zhong Huang Zhi Xiang (Fenghuang Dancong line)
processing: Made as a Fenghuang Dancong: as with other teas of the area, the leaf is withered, bruised and partly oxidised, then fixed, rolled into long strips and dried with a roast.
harvest_season: Fenghuang Dancong is mainly a spring tea; the exact picking dates of this line are not well recorded.
appearance_dry: Heavy, tightly made strips, dark brown and glossy.
appearance_wet: As with other Dancong, long leaves that open fully; the line is known for leaves a little broader and more oval than its relatives.
taste_profile: Natural floral aroma, gardenia by repute, with a full, smooth body, a honeyed mountain character and a long sweet return that lasts through many steeps.

brewing.notes: Dancong turns bitter quickly, so use a light hand and pour off fast. This tea is prized for stamina; a small dose goes a long way.

vintage_note: As with other Fenghuang Dancong, it is normally sold by spring harvest of the current year, often after a period of rest following the roast. The original tree is reported dead, so anything on sale should come from propagated plants, and a claim of mother-tree leaf should be doubted. Ask which generation of plants and which village it comes from.
description:
Song Zhong No. 1 is one of the famous names of Fenghuang Dancong, tied to a single very old tea tree at Lizaiping on Wudong mountain, about 1,150 m up. It usually goes by another name, Song Zhong Huang Zhi Xiang, and many drinkers know it as Dong Fang Hong.

The name matters less than the idea: a whole line of tea descended from one plant. Villagers multiplied it first by layering and later by cuttings, so what reaches the cup today comes from those descendants, grown and made in the usual Fenghuang way.

The cup is described as golden and full, with a natural floral scent, a honeyed mountain character and a sweetness that keeps returning. It is known for lasting: long after an ordinary oolong has gone flat, this should still give something. Keep the steeps short, because Dancong punishes a slow pour.

Be careful when buying. Song Zhong is a name with prestige, and it is applied loosely. Other old trees also carry the Song Zhong name, such as the Da'an tree, and these are different teas. Ask the seller which line and village the leaf comes from, and treat any talk of the original tree with suspicion.
history:
Local accounts place the tree's selection in the late Southern Song by a villager named Li. That origin is tradition rather than record, and the age given varies between more than 600 and more than 700 years. Accounts also differ on whether Song Zhong No. 1 and the Song Zhong Huang Zhi Xiang mother tree are strictly the same plant, though they are generally treated together.

One detailed account lists a long run of names: Yan Shang Zhen in 1946 at a Fenghuang merchant's shop in Vietnam, Huang Zhi Xiang in 1956 for its gardenia-like scent, Dong Fang Hong in 1969, and a return to Song Zhong around 1980. Cuttings were taken in 1962, which widened the planting.

The same account says the Song Zhong No. 1 tree, put at over 700 years old, died in 2016 and is kept at the Chaozhou Fenghuang Dancong tea museum. It separately describes finding a centuries-old Song Zhong Huang Zhi Xiang tree leafless in 2017, blaming heavy picking and foot traffic that packed the soil; it does not say whether this is the same tree.
